This is gonna be a lengthy review. I'll add a TL;DR at the bottom.

When I first went to view the page for this game, there were many questions that began flooding my mind. And now that I've played the game almost to its entirety, I think that I can answer most of these questions that interested consumers passing by may have. This game was a real treat, and I think that it deserves more attention than it's received.


[h1] Is Hacknet realistic? [/h1]

If you mean "realistic" as in "Is this game close to hacking in real life?" then the answer is no. This game is not realistic because it is fun and doesn't make you paranoid. You are in possession of a bunch of hacking tools that put up the kinds of graphics you'd expect to be running on computers in a 90's hacker film, and the way these tools work is by executing them and waiting for the flashy hacking graphics to stop flashing so that you can run another flashy hacker tool until you gain administrative system access. Granted, it's more complex than that, which is why this game is really enjoyable, but you're not going to be writing complex algorithms to overload proxy servers and bypass tracing measures. That's what the 90's tools are for.

That being said, this may be as close as gaming will ever come to realistic hacking. Because anything that tries to be precicely like real hacking that doesn't give you fancy hacker programs probably isn't going to be a very fun game. And this, again, is a fun game. The entire game takes place on a computer's operating system, and every hack you perform is done through this system. In addition, the commands you use are based on real UNIX commands, even if the commands are typically used to activate the previously-mentioned hacking programs. It's certainly more realistic than games where you push a button and your character goes [i]"I'm in" [/i] like Watch_Dogs and Quadrilateral Cowboy (That isn't to say that they're bad games, just that they're not trying to be realistic hacking simulations which, again, isn't necessarily a bad thing).


[h1] Is this game immersive? Will I feel like a hacker even if I'm not performing real hacks? [/h1]

Oh, yes. If you want to feel like the genius hacker that always appears in Hollywood films but rarely gets any time for actual character development, then this game is for you. The presentation of this game is great, and it really helps to sell that feeling of accomplishment that you get when you pull off a successful job. After about 30 minutes in, I had to re-check the steam store to make sure that I wasn't accessing a multiplayer hacking simulator. But nope, I was even able to play this game in airplane mode. As the store page mentions, there are very few things that break the immersion by being obvious parts of a video game. To complete a job, you email the client explaining that you've finished. To acquire a new tool, you have to copy said tool to your home computer from its rightful owner. 

And this immersive presentation goes a long way in the overall experience. I know that not everybody responds the same way, but I found certain parts to incite genuine emotion in a way that few other games have managed to pull off. Like when you're given the option to accept a job in which [spoiler]you have to euthanize a dying man by hacking his pacemaker [/spoiler], or when [spoiler]you run "OpenCDtray" on your own system and your real computer's disc tray opens and may potentially scare the hell out of you[/spoiler]. So even if you're using overpowered tools to open systems that nobody bothers to check, you'll probably still feel really good doing so.


[h1] Do I need to know coding or hacking in order to understand this game? [/h1]

No, you don't. The tutorial explains everything pretty well, and it makes sure that you understand how the systems work before even thinking about letting you out into the hacking world. No coding is required (I'm not even sure if coding algorithms is possible with the interface), and most of the game's difficulty comes with memorizing the commands and executing them at the appropriate times. That being said, if you don't know a whole lot about computers, the most difficult task will probably be [spoiler] getting your interface back after being locked to terminal mode by another hacker [/spoiler]. But if you experiment enough, then you'll ususally find the solutions to most of the challenges, and there are plenty of walkthroughs and tips out there if you end up getting desperate. But I was able to finish the game with little prior programming experience. If you know how to navigate a computer's interface or have downloaded and fixed mods on to other games, then you'll probably be fine with this game. Just, you know, don't delete important files or screw up on a trace aversion. I don't know if this game prevents you from screwing yourself over, and everybody's too scared to find out.


[h1] Is the game worth ten bucks? [/h1]

Yeah, I'd say so. You'll probably get around 10 hours out of it if you're doing the main story without any outside assitance, 14-15 hours if you're also doing the labrynths DLC. I'd say that it's not everybody's cup of tea; surely, your relative who spends all day exclusively playing [i] Fortnite [/i] would probably get turned off by this, but odds are you're at least mildly interested in this game if you're reading this review right now, considering that this game gets talked about as much as what brand of toilet paper you prefer when you're finished up on the toilet. So yeah, I'd recommend this game to anybody reading this review.


[h1] Oh, boy. It's one of those games that tries to sell its soundtrack as DLC. Is it good enough to warrant a purchase? [/h1]

I was honestly surprised by this game's soundtrack. Again, I understand that everybody has different tastes in music, but I found this particular OST track good to write and do homework to. It felt really good to listen to in-game while hacking servers and computers. The music is used as sort of an indicator on what part of the game you're currently at, and when the song changes, you know you're probably making progress. I found that [spoiler] Roller Mobster by Carpenter Brut [/spoiler] fit this game better than it did for HM2. That being said, I haven't purchased the soundtrack since most of it is available on YouTube anyways. And yes, it's ten dollars. Fifteen dollars for the main game and DLC soundtrack. So while I'll admit that the soundtrack is pretty good, I'd only spend the extra fifteen bucks if you like having the songs directly at your fingertips at all times.


[h1] TL;DR [/h1]

This is a great game that may be as close to realistic hacking as gaming will come while still remaining enjoyable. The presentation and aeshetic really add a lot to it, and you don't need to be experienced with programming or hacking in order to complete it. It's worth the money and gives around 10 hours of playtime assuming you don't mess up massively and have to start a new game. I'm gonna give this a thumbs up, and I wish it came out later so that I could put it in my favorite 2018 games list.

I’ll admit it, I wasn’t expecting Hacknet to be very good. I had heard of it through friends and didn’t think it would actually be that good of a game. A few months ago it was on sale for about $2 and I thought, “I’ll get it bc it’s cheap and on my wishlist.” I then proceeded to not even download the game until today....when I played it for 8.3 hours straight.

Hacknet is a beautiful “narrative” that is so entertaining. The soundtrack, gameplay, puzzles, and little secrets make it probably one of my favorite games.

The Gameplay:
I hope you’re ready to type a lot (and click a lot too depending on how you navigate) because Hacknet, as advertised, is a terminal based game, almost every action you want to do just me typed out. I’m not upset by this at all, it makes it feel much more real and at certain times *cough* endgame *cough* you feel like you’re in a movie, your fingers flying across the keyboard as you’re starting your programs, flying through files, all while the clock is ticking down.
I’m not sure how the Hacknet devs did it, but they created a super immersive game out of a “typing simulator.” They make you feel the rush when the trace timer is counting down and the screen flashes red. Or the panic when you’re trying to save your computer after you get traced. Or the absolute blind rage and confusion when your computer crashes when you enter a command wrong— oh wait, that’s just the in-game computer, phew.

The Story:
Hacknet might not seem like much of a narrative to most, but I’d put Hacknet up there with Stanley Parable, Beginners Guide, and Firewatch (as well as other amazing narratives I haven’t played yet). The story is you trying to find out what happens to the hacker Bit. While the mid section of the game is mostly you honing your skills and messing around, there are still strange things going on..... I will say, I’m not a fan of the whole “if you’re reading this, that means I’m already dead” cliché. The beginning of the game and the end all drive that point home and while I don’t think the game would be the same without it, I do feel like a different twist would be nice.
-Story side notes: Read the IRC logs, those are some of the funniest “chats” I’ve read. They add some light hearted humor as well as some humanity amongst the chaos.

The Soundtrack:
By far my favorite soundtrack since Mirror’s Edge: Catalyst. Despite Hacknet only having about 8-10 songs, they are driven by story cues and fit well. They do repeat until you progress and while that can get annoying, yet I find myself tapping my foot or bobbing my head to the beat while I’m blasting my keyboard apart with my fingers. The best part of the game/soundtrack is when the endgame starts. I’ve never gotten so hyped but in such a zone before in my life. 

The Issues:
I didn’t really have too many problems with this game. Some resolution scaling issues at the beginning when I accidentally switched from the stock resolution but that’s about it. Some “digging” was a challenge, I reached multiple roadblocks towards the endgame and I had to look up some walkthroughs to see what I was missing but then after I got unstuck I was back at it.

The Summary:
I love this game, and I’d play it again. I love everything about the game. It’s aesthetically pleasing, the audio is fantastic, the soundtrack is fantastic, the “controls” are a bit of a learning curve at first but you’ll pick them up quickly, and the story is phenomenal.

This game is on a whole new level. Not many ambitious games like this can simultaneously achieve what they were hoping for (a realistic hacking sim) and make it fundamentally a good standalone game. You could have an accurate farming simulator, but then fail to make it fun with poor progression and pacing, or vice versa. This game doesn't compromise; it does both and does them well.

So for the recommendation part, here's a quick list of the good and bad (minimal spoilers).

Pros: 
[list]
    [*] One of the most comprehensive/accurate hacking sim games out there (rejoice, UNIX users)
    [*] Designed for beginners and the experienced alike
    [*] Great music, atmosphere, story, and of course gameplay
    [*] Fun puzzles, with good but not overly instrusive prompts
    [*] Replayability with some randomisations (expect 2-5 playthroughs for non-DLC)
    [*] Multiple routes, and many secrets
    [*] Everything links to each other (secrets, stories/lore, hints,)
    [*] Great community and moderators, if you ever need help
[/list]

Cons:
[list]
    [*] Not all missions may have the best "turn-in" trigger hints, but you can always consult the friendly community
    [*] Due to the complexities of data sanitisation in a game like this, not "everything" is technically possible (you can still do some fun stuff, just not literal programming inside the files)
    [*] Possible to get softlocked in many places; just dont stray off too far off the course and rm * every server lol
    [*] Singleplayer, because multiplayer turned out to be overly amibtious (even for this dev) and severly was underplayed
    [*] Existance of an awesome GUI may break the illusion of a "truly accurate" hacking sim, making it seem more like a script kiddie simulator, but I think this is justified for keeping the game immersive and fun for everyone
[/list]

I'll start here by saying I got this game when HumbleBundle ran a promotion that allowed me to get it for free, but even with that said, I would definitely pay $10 for it after having played it.  I was expecting it to be a quirky little hacking simulator that would just be fun to play around with for a bit, but then I jumped into it and got an UNEXPECTEDLY DEEP game.  There is a well-developed and engaging storyline, and combined with the excellent soundtrack, it is an exceptionally immersive game where you feel like what you do actually matters.  The principle is simple enough: you're a hacker, and you're doing hacker things.  But all the hacker things that you do actually have a purpose in advancing the story, which is very nicely written.  It's a quick little game - you can probably beat it in just a few hours, to be honest - but the fact that it supports Steam Workshop content means there's no lack of new things to add to the experience.  A good one to catch on sale, but I'd also say it's well worth the full price!

This game very obviously has taken a lot of inspiration form Uplink. It has added some of it's own creativity, but also removed some of the good stuff from uplink.

Some of the puzzles weren't challenging enough and some of the mechanics were silly. For example you hack directly from your machine without routing through any other proxy to prevent counter trace. Yet early in the game you get attacked by another hacker and he bounces his connection through other machines. Maybe the developers intended to have this but had to cut it out due to crunch.

The game is pretty scripted. If you leave logs I don't think you get hacked back. However scripted NPCs will hack you back very hard / quick. 

They have also removed the concept of money and upgrades compared to UpLink. WHY??

The contract servers are also very scripted .. it's not a 'world' where other entities, histories, bank accounts, machines exist on their own apart from the story line. You can't just go off and do contracts for a while, accumulate money and explore around. This is another change from UpLink.

The machine you start with has piddly amount of 'memory' on which you can barely run 2 programs side by side. Sometimes time is of the essence and you need to do 5-6 things (defeat proxy, defeat firewall, hack ports, etc etc) and it's annoying they took out the option to upgrade your computer.

In uplink I personally loved hacking banks and watching my account go to a million .. so I miss that in this game.

On the other hand, this game is excellent when it comes to .. cutscenes. When you reach a scripted juncture and you're racign against the clock to get into a system or get out .. amazing visuals, music etc. Well done on this.

The problem with overly scripted nature is that there is no replayability or world exploration after story completion.
Overall summary:
I'd say that UpLink was REVOLUTIONARY and this game has taken that concept, removed about 10% of it (including some good stuff) and added another 35 parts to become 125% of UpLink. So this is like UpLink 1.25 for me.

It's a good game, get it and play it. Also check out UpLink if you haven't.
